mission.title: Our Mission
mission.text: So that every traveler who visits Seoul does not miss this oasis reborn from a garbage mountain inside World Cup Park, we have gathered scattered official information into this guide — purely to give you the most authentic viewing and cultural experience.

practicalInfo.title: Visitor Facilities & Practical Information
practicalInfo.subtitle: What is available on the hill and in the surrounding area, described by category so you can plan without any commercial recommendation.
practicalInfo.neutralNote: As an independent non-profit guide we do not recommend or rank individual businesses. The categories below simply describe the types of facilities you will find around the park.

groups.title: Restrooms
groups.summary: There are no restrooms at the summit. Public toilets are in the lower parks and along the Han River side.
points: The nearest public restrooms are in Peace Park below the hill and around Nanji Stream.
Some facilities include baby-changing tables and accessible stalls.
If you plan to stay on the summit, use a restroom before you start the climb.

groups.title: Parking
groups.summary: There is no large dedicated car park on the hill; park below and walk or ride the shuttle up.
points: World Cup Park's main public car park, under and beside Peace Park, has the most spaces.
A smaller temporary lot sits at the foot of the hill, with limited capacity.
Weekends and the autumn silver-grass season fill up fast — public transport is usually easier.

groups.title: Food & Drink
groups.summary: There is no restaurant or shop on the summit. Eat in the lower park area or in the nearby districts.
points: Kiosks, convenience stores and cafés around Peace Park and the Han River side cover light meals.
The surrounding neighbourhoods offer a wide range of restaurants, noodle shops and bakeries.
Open fires and barbecues are not permitted anywhere in the park.

groups.title: Where to Stay
groups.summary: The park itself has no accommodation; lodging is concentrated in nearby districts and the city centre.
points: Around the park you will mostly find business hotels, guesthouses and hostels.
Riverside hotels along the Han River suit travellers who want a water view.
Rates rise sharply in the spring and autumn peak seasons — book ahead.

groups.title: Shops & Supplies
groups.summary: No large stores inside the park; convenience stores and supermarkets are near the stations and residential blocks.
points: Convenience stores near the subway station and residential areas sell water, snacks and rain gear.
Supermarkets and fresh-food markets in the surrounding districts are good for stocking up.
The summit is dry and windy — carry more water than you expect to need.

groups.title: Fuel & EV Charging
groups.summary: No fuel or charging facilities inside the park; these are found along the surrounding city roads.
points: Petrol stations line the main roads around the World Cup Park area.
Public car parks generally include electric-vehicle charging bays.
Check opening hours and payment methods before you rely on a particular site.

groups.title: Accessibility
groups.summary: Wheelchairs and strollers can reach the summit platform via the upper service road.
points: The park shuttle runs on fixed stops and removes the need to use the main stairway.
The boardwalk gradients are gentle and suit wheelchairs and strollers.
Ask on-site staff for assistance if you need a step-free route.

groups.title: Safety & Emergencies
groups.summary: The summit is open and exposed — watch the weather and the closing time.
points: Lighting is limited after sunset; plan to descend before dusk.
Steps become slippery in rain or ice — wear shoes with good grip.
In an emergency in Korea call 119 for ambulance and rescue, or 112 for police.

story.title: History, Stories & the Living Hill
story.subtitle: Haneul Park is more than a viewpoint. Beneath the silver grass lies one of the most remarkable environmental turnarounds in Korea — a landfill that became a public meadow.

timeline.title: The landfill opens
timeline.text: Nanjido, a sandbank in the Han River, begins receiving almost all of Seoul's household waste.

timeline.title: Fifteen years of waste
timeline.text: Roughly 92 million tonnes of refuse are stacked into two huge mounds, making it the largest landfill the country had ever seen.

timeline.title: The landfill closes
timeline.text: Waste stops arriving. The site is sealed and left to stabilise under layers of soil.

timeline.title: Ecological restoration
timeline.text: Deep soil capping and planting stabilise the slopes. Pioneer grasses, silver grass among them, colonise the bare ground.

timeline.title: World Cup Park opens
timeline.text: Ahead of the FIFA World Cup the site reopens as World Cup Park. Haneul Park is the high meadow on its north-western edge.

timeline.title: A Seoul icon
timeline.text: Autumn silver grass and sunsets over the Han River make the hill one of the city's best-loved seasonal destinations.

legends.title: Why Nanjido?
legends.text: The old name of the island is usually read as 蘭芝島, the island where orchids and fragrant grasses grew, though some explain it as 卵島, egg island, after its smooth oval outline. Either way the name records what the sandbank once was, long before it became a landfill.

legends.title: Ninety metres above the memory
legends.text: Locals still call the hill a garbage mountain. Standing on the summit with wind moving through the silver grass, it is almost impossible to believe the ground beneath your feet was once the city's refuse. The transformation is the story.

legends.title: Why the sky?
legends.text: Haneul simply means sky. The name was given to a hill that rises high enough to feel level with the clouds, and to a place meant to lift the city's gaze back up.

nature.title: Silver grass meadow
nature.text: Silver grass established itself naturally on the capped landfill and now forms the signature autumn meadow — a textbook example of ecological succession on disturbed ground.

nature.title: A stopover for birds
nature.text: Beside the Han River and Nanji Stream the park sits on a migration corridor; wetland birds and waterfowl rest here in spring and autumn.

nature.title: Insects and small wildlife
nature.text: The open meadow supports pollinators and insects through the warm months, which in turn feed the birds passing through.

nature.title: Cooling the city
nature.text: Greenery over a capped landfill stores carbon, holds the soil and eases the urban heat island — a practical lesson in circular land use.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.text: Fresh growth on the slopes, blossom along the river and migrating birds passing through.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.text: Deep green meadow, long daylight hours and warm evenings over the city skyline.

seasons.name: Autumn
seasons.text: Silver grass at its peak, the reason most travellers come, together with the year's best sunsets.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.text: A quiet, snow-dusted hill, clear air and wintering waterfowl on the river below.

hero.title: Haneul Park (하늘공원)
hero.subtitle: An ecological oasis in Seoul's Mapo-gu, inside World Cup Park — reborn from a former landfill. Free to enter, it is Seoul's top spot for silver-grass meadows, Han River sunsets and the city skyline. Climb the eco-hill and watch the afterglow spread across the skyline.

hiddenRules.title: Safety Tips for the Hill & Slopes
hiddenRules.subtitle: Haneul Park sits on an ~90 m ecological hill; the ascent stairs (the famous 'Haneul Park stairs') are steep. Know these in advance for a safe, smooth climb.

highlights.label: Stairs & gradient
highlights.note: About 291 ecological stairs from Peace Park to the summit — physically demanding. Wear comfy shoes, slow down and rest in stages.

highlights.label: Sun & wind
highlights.note: The hill is open with little shade; sunscreen and water in summer, warm layers for the strong river wind in autumn/winter. Light fades after sunset — plan ahead.

highlights.label: Night & descent
highlights.note: Some slopes have limited lighting before closing; descents stress the knees — elders and children should use the gentle loop or the eco-shuttle.

panels.q: Do I have to climb the stairs? Is there an alternative?
panels.a: The classic route is about 291 ecological stairs and fairly steep. Those with limited stamina, infants or reduced mobility can take the park's eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle) along the service road straight to the upper platform, avoiding the climb.
items: The shuttle has fixed stops and a fare; queues form in peak season — go off-peak.
Strollers and wheelchairs can reach the summit platform via the upper road.

panels.a: The park closes around sunset; light drops quickly afterwards and some slopes are dimly lit, plus the descent is hard on the knees. Start going down right after sunset, or take the last shuttle.

panels.q: Can I picnic, light a fire or fly a drone on the grass?
panels.a: The silver-grass slope is a protected zone — no stepping on, sitting on or picking the grass. The area is windy and near flight paths, so drones are prohibited without permission. Use the designated paths and take your trash with you.

complianceGuide.title: Haneul Park · Visitor & Ecological Etiquette
complianceGuide.subtitle: This is both a citizen's green space and a habitat we must protect together. Following these rules is basic respect for nature and others.

rules.title: No entering or picking the grass
rules.text: The silver-grass slope is a protected ecological zone — do not step on, sit on or pick the grass; stay on the paved paths and boardwalks.
items: Stop immediately at signs reading 'Protect the turf' or 'No entry'.
For photos, never step onto the slope or trample vegetation for a better angle.

rules.title: Take your trash with you
rules.text: Bins at the top and on the slope are limited and the wind scatters litter. Bring a small bag and take everything away when you leave.

rules.title: Quiet viewing
rules.text: Many come specifically to watch the sunset and city nightscape in silence. Before and around sunset, please lower your voice and avoid loud music.

rules.title: No smoking or open flame
rules.text: The grass is highly flammable in dry seasons — the whole park is smoke-free; no open flame, BBQ or smoking, to prevent fire.

tips: Peace Park is the gateway to World Cup Park with the best facilities and restrooms — resupply here first.

steps.title: [Stop 2] Climb Haneul Park stairs for the reeds
steps.text: Climb the 291 ecological stairs to the summit; autumn silver-grass and the dusk skyline are best. Take the eco-shuttle if low on energy.
tips: Summit 60–90 min before sunset for the best light; go early to avoid crowds.

steps.title: [Stop 3] Nanji Hangang Park cycle or stroll
steps.text: Descend west to Nanji Hangang Park; follow the Han River for wetlands, migratory birds and afterglow. Rent a public bike.

steps.title: [Stop 4] World Cup Stadium & surroundings
steps.text: Return to the stadium area; view the stadium exterior, browse culture and dining — the legacy of the 2002 World Cup.

steps.title: [End] Hongdae / Mangwon Market dinner

tips: If visiting during the silver-grass festival, focus on Haneul Park and Peace Park.

intro.title: Getting to Know Haneul Park
intro.description: Haneul Park (하늘공원, Haneul Park) sits inside World Cup Park in Seoul's Mapo-gu — an ecological park built atop the former Nanjido (난지도) landfill. '하늘' means 'sky' in Korean, and the park takes its name from the high hill that seems to touch the sky. It is both Seoul citizens' weekend green lung for climbing, reed-viewing and sunsets, and a symbol of 'waste-to-wonder' environmental regeneration — once Seoul's largest garbage mountain, now an ecological oasis where silver-grass sways and migratory birds rest.

visitGuide.title: Visitor Guide
visitGuide.description: Haneul Park is free and open daily, roughly 06:00–22:00 (seasonal). Make a dusk summit for the sunset your main plan, then link Peace Park, Nanji Hangang Park and the World Cup Stadium. The summit is open with minimal facilities — do your supplies at the foot (Peace Park) or nearby commercial areas.
items: Free and open daily; dusk summit for sunset and skyline is best for light and photos.
Best angles are the southwest slope and viewing deck; autumn silver-grass (eulalia) is most spectacular.
From Line 6 World Cup Stadium Stn (월드컵경기장) Exit 1, walk ~15 min to the foot, then climb the stairs or take the shuttle.
No shops or food at the top; water and restrooms are at the foot (Peace Park) and Nanjicheon — stock up beforehand.

transportSection.overviewText: Haneul Park is inside World Cup Park in Seoul's Mapo-gu. The easiest external link is flying into Incheon (ICN)/Gimpo (GMP) or taking the KTX to Seoul Station, then the subway. In the city, the park is next to Line 6 World Cup Stadium Stn (월드컵경기장); transferring from Line 2/AREX usually takes ~30–50 min. Haneul Park is an ~90 m eco-hill — from the foot you climb 291 stairs or take the eco-shuttle.

No large dedicated lot at the summit — use World Cup Park's public parking or nearby paid lots, then walk/shuttle up.
During the autumn reed festival and weekends crowds are heavy; parking and stairs jam — strongly prefer transit or off-peak.

officialManagement.title: About the Park
officialManagement.text: Haneul Park is an ecological park in Seoul's Mapo-gu, inside World Cup Park, transformed from the former Nanjido landfill and managed by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as urban green space. Long a public place for citizens to climb, view reeds and watch the sunset, it is also a symbol of 'resource cycling' and 'environmental regeneration' for the city.

humanities.title: History & Transformation
humanities.subtitle: Following the landfill closure, ecological regeneration and on-site signs, we present the history of Haneul Park — from garbage mountain to urban oasis.

sections.title: From garbage mountain to Haneul Park
sections.content: Nanjido (난지도), where Haneul Park stands, was Seoul's largest landfill from 1978 to 1993, receiving most of the city's household waste in mounds tens of meters high. After closure, the city stabilized the hill with thick soil cover and grass, and leveraged the 2002 Korea-Japan World Cup to promote environmental regeneration — opening in 1999 as part of 'World Cup Park' under the name 'Haneul Park'. '하늘 (sky)' refers both to its towering height and to the city's upward transformation.

sections.title: Closure & ecological regeneration
sections.content: After closure, soil and vegetation gradually stabilized the hill, and pioneer plants such as silver-grass (eulalia) naturally colonized it into a unique upland meadow. Today it is not only a rare urban meadow in Seoul but also a stopover for migratory birds and a window for stargazing and sunset — the once foul-smelling garbage mountain has become the city's 'green lung'.

sections.title: Part of World Cup Park
sections.content: Haneul Park forms 'World Cup Park' together with Peace Park, Pyeonghwa (Peace) Park, Nakji (Orchid) Park, Noeul (Sunset) Park and Haneul (Sky) Park — a representative environmental regeneration landmark of Seoul. It weaves 'waste treatment — ecological restoration — public recreation' into a readable urban narrative.

sections.title: Stairs & ecological design
sections.content: The park reaches the summit via the famous 291 ecological stairs, preserving the ritual of climbing while also serving elders, children and the less mobile — an upper service road carries the eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle). The grass is ringed by boardwalks to minimize trampling, a model of 'low-impact development'.

sections.title: Citizens' sky living room
sections.content: Today Haneul Park has shifted from a barren hill to an urban green space anyone can reach. Free and open, it draws morning exercisers and dusk sunset-watchers, and during the autumn reed festival becomes a citywide event — a node where Seoul's daily life and tourism meet.

sections.title: A symbol of Seoul's regeneration
sections.content: From garbage mountain to oasis, Haneul Park is seen as a spiritual corner of Seoul's urban transformation and sustainable development, echoing the global 'waste-to-wonder' narrative. It reminds us that great urban landmarks often come from a gentler treatment of the land.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Nanjido, where Haneul Park stands, received most of Seoul's household waste from 1978 to 1993, with mounds tens of meters high. Today, covered in soil and greenery, the autumn silver-grass ripples in the wind — few would guess a garbage mountain lies beneath their feet.

sitePlaques.title: Reading the On-site Signs
sitePlaques.subtitle: When you visit, official signs and maps at the foot and summit are the most authoritative first-hand source on its regeneration history. We translate and explain each one.
sitePlaques.intro: The following readings are based on on-site photos of the Seoul Metropolitan Government's regeneration signs, ecological maps and shuttle instructions.

items.title: Nanjido landfill & World Cup Park regeneration
items.koTitleZh: Nanjido Landfill & World Cup Park Development
items.body: The sign records: Nanjido was Seoul's largest household-waste landfill (1978–1993); after closure it was ecologically restored with soil cover and greenery, and World Cup Park was built for the 2002 Korea-Japan World Cup. Haneul Park opened in 1999 as part of it — a public green space for citizens to climb and view the river.

items.title: Silver-grass, birds & meadow ecology
items.body: The bilingual eco sign explains: the Haneul Park meadow naturally succeeded after landfill soil cover, with silver-grass (eulalia) as the dominant pioneer plant; in autumn the reeds turn snow-white, and in spring/summer it hosts insects and migratory birds — reminding visitors not to enter the slope and to protect it together.

items.title: Stairs, boardwalk & eco-shuttle
items.body: The park map marks: 291 ecological stairs to the summit; an upper road for the eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle) with fixed stops and a fare; the grass ringed by boardwalks, with wheelchairs and strollers reaching the summit platform via the upper road. Note last-departure times and suspension in bad weather.

gallery.title: Photo Gallery
gallery.subtitle: From silver-grass meadows, Han River sunsets and the city skyline to four-season slopes — see the visual beauty of Haneul Park.

reviews.title: Visitor Reviews
reviews.declaration: Visitor feedback is available on Google Maps (external link).
reviews.featuredSubtitle: A few short lines that capture the spirit of Haneul Park.

featured.text: At the summit at dusk, the whole Seoul skyline lit up by afterglow with the scent of reeds on the wind — truly healing.
The autumn silver-grass blankets the slope like snow, free and overlooking the Han River — Seoul's gentlest sunset spot.
Took the eco-shuttle up with the kids, skipping the 291 stairs — easy even for the elders.

items.name: Minjun
items.text: Summited before sunset; the afterglow lit the skyline and the place went quiet — strongly recommend dusk, best light.

items.name: Seoyeon
items.text: Open slope, great views; the shuttle is family-friendly, but the top is windy so dress warm.

items.name: Jihun
items.text: Worth it as a free city park; the 291 stairs are a real workout — take the shuttle if not fit.

items.name: Ha-eun
items.text: About 15 min walk from World Cup Stadium Stn; Peace Park on the way is lovely for a half-day stroll.

stairs.title: Haneul Park Stairs vs. the Frog Tram (개구리차)
stairs.subtitle: No private car can reach the summit. You either climb the zigzag stairway or ride the park's frog tram — here is the honest comparison to help you choose.

stairsCard.title: Zigzag Stairs
items: 291 ecological stairs zigzag from Peace Park up the ~90 m eco-hill.
On foot it takes about 15–20 minutes at a steady pace, or 25–30 minutes with photo stops.
Free, and open with the park (roughly 06:00–22:00, seasonal).
Steep with no ramp — not suitable for strollers or wheelchairs.

tramCard.title: Frog Tram (개구리차)
items: A rubber-tyred shuttle climbs the service road to the upper platform; from there it is a ~5 minute walk to the summit.
About ₩3,000 for an adult round trip (≈ ₩2,000 one way), with reduced fares for children — confirm current rates at the booth.
The accessible option for elders, small children, strollers and wheelchairs.
Runs on fixed stops; queues are longest during the autumn silver-grass festival and on weekend afternoons.

stairs.verdict: If you are reasonably fit and want the classic Haneul Park experience, take the stairs up and — especially after sunset — consider the tram for the descent to spare your knees. With elders, infants or a stroller, use the frog tram in both directions. On peak autumn weekends, walking up is often faster than waiting in the tram queue.
stairs.disclaimer: Tram fares, routes and closing times are set by the park operator and can change; please confirm at the ticket booth or the official Seoul parks site before you go.

sunset.title: Best Sunset & Photo Spots in Haneul Park
sunset.subtitle: Haneul Park faces due west over the Han River, so the whole western rim of the summit turns gold at dusk. These are the viewpoints and timings photographers rely on.

spots.name: West Rim Observation Deck (한강 조망대)
spots.text: The main sunset platform on the Han River side — an unobstructed frame of the river, Nanji Hangang Park and the skyline behind it. On weekends, arrive and claim a spot 40–60 minutes early.

spots.name: Silver-grass Boardwalk
spots.text: The boardwalks threading the eulalia meadow are the signature foreground: backlit silver-grass with the sunset behind. October–November is peak, when the meadow turns pink-muhly and gold.

spots.name: North Slope toward Noeul Park
spots.text: Looking north-west, the neighbouring Noeul (Sunset) Park ridge and the World Cup Stadium roof catch the last light — a quieter alternative to the main deck.

spots.name: Summit Pavilion & Lawn
spots.text: The open lawn near the pavilion is where you spread a mat, shoot silhouettes and wait for the blue hour — the ~30 minutes after sunset when the sky turns deep blue and city lights switch on.

timingItems: Arrive at the summit about 60 minutes before sunset to walk the rim and pick a spot.
The best light runs from roughly 40 minutes before sunset through the blue hour (~30 minutes after).
Peak season is the Seoul Silver-grass Festival, mid-October to mid-November, when the meadow is densest and crowds are largest.
Summer sunsets fall around 19:30–20:00, winter around 17:00–17:30 — check the live sunset time at the top of this page.
Bring a light jacket: the exposed summit is a few degrees cooler and windier than the city below.
photoItems: Shoot wide for the meadow-plus-city frame, then switch to a longer lens to compress the skyline at dusk.
Never step off the boardwalk or trample the silver-grass for a better angle — rangers do enforce it.
A small tripod is fine on the platform but keep paths clear; it helps for blue-hour cityscapes.

nearbyDayTrip.title: Haneul Park & Nearby Attractions: A Mapo-gu Day Trip
nearbyDayTrip.subtitle: Haneul Park sits in the middle of a cluster of western-Seoul highlights. Pair it with the Oil Tank Culture Park and Nanji Hangang Park for a full, low-effort day.

stops.name: Haneul Park (하늘공원)
stops.text: Begin at the World Cup Stadium foot, climb the 291 stairs or take the frog tram, then walk the silver-grass meadow and the Han River overlook. Allow 2–3 hours at an easy pace.

stops.name: Oil Tank Culture Park (문화비축기지)
stops.text: Five former oil storage tanks, a 15-minute walk from the World Cup Stadium, have been reborn as a free culture park with exhibitions, a rooftop viewpoint and a café inside a tank. It is the closest major sight to Haneul Park and pairs perfectly with the stadium area.

stops.name: Nanji Hangang Park (난지한강공원)
stops.text: Walk or cycle west to the Han River for wetlands, migratory-bird viewpoints, riverside lawns and bike rentals. The riverside sunset here follows on naturally from the Haneul Park view and is a relaxed way to end the day.

stops.name: World Cup Stadium & Hongdae
stops.text: Finish at the Seoul World Cup Stadium concourse, then ride one or two subway stops to Hongdae or Mangwon Market for street food and nightlife.

tips: Do the whole loop on foot in 4–6 hours, or rent a public bike at Nanji Hangang Park to shorten the riverside stretch.
Haneul Park and the Oil Tank Culture Park are both free; only the frog tram inside Haneul Park charges a fare.
Short on time? Prioritise Haneul Park + the Oil Tank Culture Park — they are a 15-minute walk apart.
Check the sunset time before you start so you are on the Haneul Park summit for golden hour.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Practical info about Haneul Park's facilities, history and visit planning.

items.label: Parking
items.value: World Cup Park combined / foot lot

items.q: Is there parking, and what are the rates?
items.a: No large dedicated lot at the summit, but World Cup Park combined parking (Peace Park underground/surface, public rates) and the foot temporary lot are reachable, then walk or take the eco-shuttle. Rates vary by season; they fill fast on weekends/peak, so arrive early or prefer transit.

items.q: Are wheelchairs or strollers allowed in the area?
items.a: The summit platform and upper road are reachable by the eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle), so wheelchairs and strollers can reach the upper viewing area; but the classic 291 stairs are steep with no ramp — the lower-to-upper move needs the shuttle. The boardwalks are gentle and good for pushing.

items.q: Are there restrooms or food at the site?
items.a: The summit slope has no shops or food; the nearest water and public toilets are at the foot (Peace Park), Nanjicheon and the combined parking (~10–15 min walk back). Stock up before going up.

items.q: Why is it called 'Haneul (Sky)', and does it relate to the garbage mountain?
items.a: '하늘' means sky; the park sits on an ~90 m eco-hill that seems to touch the sky, hence 'Haneul Park'. Its predecessor was Seoul's largest Nanjido landfill — the name and the land together tell a regeneration story from garbage mountain to oasis.

items.q: What is special about its ecology and landform?
items.a: After landfill closure and soil cover, pioneer plants like silver-grass naturally formed a meadow — now a stopover for migratory birds and a window for stargazing and sunset; the stairs-plus-shuttle design is also a model of 'low-impact development' and sustainability.

items.q: Is Haneul Park free to enter?
items.a: Yes — entry is completely free. Haneul Park is a public ecological park inside World Cup Park with no gate, no admission fee and no reservation required. Only the internal frog tram (개구리차) charges a separate fare. Opening hours are roughly 06:00–22:00, varying by season.

items.q: How much are the Haneul Park tram (frog tram) tickets?
items.a: The frog tram (개구리차) that climbs the service road to the upper platform costs about ₩3,000 for an adult round trip (≈ ₩2,000 one way), with reduced fares for children; fares are paid at the booth and are separate from entry, which is free. Rates, routes and operating hours are set by the park and can change, so confirm on site.

items.q: How many stairs are there in Haneul Park?
items.a: There are 291 ecological stairs zigzagging from the foot (Peace Park) to the summit — about a 15–20 minute climb at a steady pace. They are steep with no ramp, so visitors with strollers, wheelchairs or limited mobility should use the frog tram up the service road instead.

items.q: How long does a visit take?
items.a: A typical summit takes about 1–2 hours (stairs/shuttle plus time at the top); allow half a day if adding Peace Park, Nanji Hangang Park and the World Cup Stadium.

items.q: Can I still go in bad weather?
items.a: Yes — it is an open park, visitable in any weather. But the summit slope is windy; in thunderstorms or snow it gets slippery with low visibility — wear grippy shoes, watch the weather and closing time; the eco-shuttle may suspend in bad weather.

items.q: After visiting, what other attractions are worth it?
items.a: From Haneul Park you can link Peace Park, Nakji (Orchid) Park, Nanji Hangang Park (wetlands & cycling), the Seoul World Cup Stadium, and farther out Hongdae/Mangwon Market and Yeouido Hangang Park — a half-day 'eco–culture–food' line in western Seoul.

scienceArt.title: Architecture & Regeneration of Haneul Park: Stairs, Meadow & Shuttle
scienceArt.subtitle: Haneul Park is more than a sunset spot — it is public heritage weaving environmental regeneration, urban design and ecological succession. Two angles to read it.

scienceMuseum.name: Stairs & Meadow
scienceMuseum.role: An eco-park built on a landfill
scienceMuseum.highlight: The park reaches the summit via 291 ecological stairs, with an upper road for the eco-shuttle; the grass is ringed by boardwalks to minimize trampling. The structure follows the hill and wind — plain and practical, harmonizing with the silver-grass meadow into a harmonious urban mountain scene, a vivid example of 'low-impact development'.
points: Siting: an ~90 m eco-hill, summit overlooks the Han River and Seoul skyline.
Structure: stairs + shuttle road + boardwalks, balancing ritual and accessibility.
Materials: soil cover and greenery, local and durable.

artMuseum.name: Reeds & Sunset
artMuseum.role: A cultural symbol of Seoul's regeneration
artMuseum.highlight: 'Haneul Park' comes from its sky-touching height, yet its predecessor was Seoul's largest landfill. From foul hill to silver-grass oasis, this transformation made it Seoul's 'waste-to-wonder' urban image and citizens' gentlest sunset memory.
points: Image: reeds, sunset and skyline — among Seoul's most recognizable urban-nature scenes.
Status: an environmental regeneration landmark of World Cup Park.
Narrative: a cultural link joining landfill, meadow and citizens' memory.

outdoorMuseum.title: Photo & Shooting Guide: Haneul Park Spots
outdoorMuseum.subtitle: As Seoul's most recognizable urban-nature landmark, a few structured spots and times greatly boost your photos' usefulness and beauty.

items.name: Sunset · skyline
items.background: Summit 60–90 min before sunset and wait for the sun to set behind the skyline across the Han. Frame with the meadow as foreground and the city as extension — Haneul Park's classic 'sunset' composition.
points: Use the meadow as foreground, place the skyline in the upper third.
Crouch low to layer the grass and afterglow for a steadier frame.

items.name: Silver-grass meadow
items.background: In autumn (usually October) the silver-grass turns snow-white; backlight makes the plumes glow, while frontlight captures the whole meadow's texture.
points: Side backlight in the morning gives the softest plume texture.
Mind the boardwalk; do not step onto the protected slope.

items.name: City nightscape
items.background: After sunset the sky warms and the city lights turn on; the blue moment (20–30 min after sunset) balances sky and lights — the most atmospheric window.
points: Shoot in the blue moment for balanced sky and city color.
Silhouette the grass, leaving a large warm skyline.

items.name: Stairs & boardwalk
items.background: Looking back from the foot at the 291 stairs, or along the boardwalk including the meadow and Han River in a wider frame — good for a closing wide shot.
points: Use the stairs as a leading line toward the summit.
Morning mist gives best layers; small aperture for full panorama.

education.title: Why did a garbage mountain become Haneul Park? (Meaning of Regeneration)
education.subtitle: A small hill built on garbage — why did it cross eras to become Seoul's environmental symbol? Behind it are layered narratives of waste, land and city memory.

points.title: Origin of waste and land
points.text: Nanjido received most of Seoul's household waste, mounds tens of meters high; after closure the city reborn the land most gently, and Haneul Park is the start of that restoration.

points.title: Citizens' sky corridor
points.text: As part of World Cup Park, it shifted from barren hill to an urban green space anyone can reach, carrying Seoul citizens' daily life of climbing, river-viewing and rest.

points.title: A link of memory
points.text: The same hill connects landfill history, meadow ecology, and today's sunset and skyline. It reminds us: great urban landmarks are often where history and reality coexist.

audience.title: Who Finds Resonance Here? (Audience Guide)
audience.subtitle: Different visitors each find their best 'way in'.

items.resonance: Free, open and safe urban green space; kids can see reeds, view the Han River and easily summit by eco-shuttle.
items.tip: Take the shuttle up; combine Peace Park lawn and Nanji Hangang cycling — adjust order by stamina.

items.resonance: Dusk sunset and city nightscape are Seoul's most romantic frames, with high shot rates.
items.tip: Secure the summit deck 60–90 min before sunset; shoot blue moment for both lights and sky color.

items.resonance: As a meadow sample reborn from a landfill, the silver-grass succession and migratory birds are worth a close look.
items.tip: Link Haneul Park with Nanji Hangang wetlands into an 'urban ecology tour'.

items.resonance: No need to go far — observe reed meadows and Han River sunsets right in Seoul; also link subway, the World Cup Stadium and local food — the ideal start to understand Seoul's urban transformation.
items.tip: Take Line 6 to World Cup Stadium Stn, then walk/shuttle.

lodging.title: Stay Guide: Near the Park, or Convenient?
lodging.subtitle: Seoul is a city 'where river meets city'. We do not recommend specific hotels, but help you read two lodging patterns to choose what fits you.

options.name: Hongdae / Hapjeong (Mapo core)
options.highlight: Stay in Hongdae or Hapjeong and Line 6 and AREX are at your door, making Haneul Park, the World Cup Stadium and Yeouido easy; the night street food and craft markets suit young travelers. Best for those focused on 'city roam + eco park' with high convenience.
points: To Haneul Park by subway ~15–30 min, one transfer.
Dining, shopping and nightlife extremely rich.
More choices, usually better value.

options.name: Mapo / Yeouido riverside
options.highlight: Stay along the Han in Mapo or Yeouido; morning riverside walks and cycling, then subway to Haneul Park. Best for those focused on 'river, sunset, slow family trips'.
points: Han River Park and bike paths at your door, good for mornings and families.
Quieter than Hongdae, good for rest.
To Haneul Park by subway ~20–30 min.

lodging.peak: In Seoul's spring/autumn peak (especially the October reed festival and April cherry season) and holidays, rooms tighten as tourists flood in and prices rise clearly. Book weeks ahead; if booking near a holiday, widen the search to Jongno, Gangnam and other areas, then take the subway back.
tips: For sunset: prefer Mapo/Yeouido riverside, river views morning and dusk.
For convenience and nightlife: choose Hongdae/Hapjeong, transit and dining at hand.
Before booking, confirm breakfast, parking and EV chargers (key for drivers).
In peak season and holidays plan ahead to avoid no-room or high prices.
